source.module_title: Keil and Delitzsch Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.13.1-Gen.13.4">Gen 13:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen206" type="x-p"/> Abram, having returned from Egypt to the south of Canaan with his wife and property uninjured, through the gracious protection of God, proceeded with Lot למסּעיו “<hi type="italic">according</hi> <hi type="italic">to his journeys</hi>” (lit., with the repeated breaking up of his camp, required by a nomad life; on נסע to break up a tent, to remove, see <reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Exo 12:37</reference>) into the neighbourhood of Bethel and Ai, where he had previously encamped and built an altar (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.8">Gen 12:8</reference>), that he might there call upon the name of the Lord again. That ויּקרא (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.4">Gen 13:4</reference>) is not a continuation of the relative clause, but a resumption of the main sentence, and therefore corresponds with ויּלך (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.3">Gen 13:3</reference>), “<hi type="italic">he went...and called upon the name of the Lord there,</hi>” has been correctly concluded by <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi> from the repetition of the subject Abram.
entries.content_plain:
Gen 13:1-4 
 
 Abram, having returned from Egypt to the south of Canaan with his wife and property uninjured, through the gracious protection of God, proceeded with Lot למסּעיו “according to his journeys” (lit., with the repeated breaking up of his camp, required by a nomad life; on נסע to break up a tent, to remove, see Exo 12:37) into the neighbourhood of Bethel and Ai, where he had previously encamped and built an altar (Gen 12:8), that he might there call upon the name of the Lord again. That ויּקרא (Gen 13:4) is not a continuation of the relative clause, but a resumption of the main sentence, and therefore corresponds with ויּלך (Gen 13:3), “he went...and called upon the name of the Lord there,” has been correctly concluded by Delitzsch from the repetition of the subject Abram.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.13.5-Gen.13.7">Gen 13:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen207" type="x-p"/> But as Abram was very rich (כּבד, lit., <hi type="italic">weighty</hi>) in possessions (מקנה, <hi type="italic">cattle and slaves</hi>), and Lot also had flocks, and herds, and tents אהלים for אהלים, <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §93, 6, 3) for his men, of whom there must have been many therefore, the land <hi type="italic">did not bear them when dwelling together</hi> (נשׁא, <hi type="italic">masculine</hi> at the commencement of the sentence, as is often the case when the verb precedes the subject, vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §147), i.e., the land did not furnish space enough for the numerous herd to graze. Consequently disputes arose between the two parties of herdsmen. The difficulty was increased by the fact that the Canaanites and Perizzites were then dwelling in the land, so that the space was very contracted. The <hi type="italic">Perizzites</hi>, who are mentioned here and in <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference>; Jdg 1:4, along with the Canaanites, and who are placed in the other lists of the inhabitants of Canaan among the different Canaanitish tribes (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.20">Gen 15:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.17">Exo 3:17</reference>, etc.), are not mentioned among the descendants of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.15-Gen.10.17">Gen 10:15-17</reference>), and may therefore, like the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, and Rephaim (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.19-Gen.15.21">Gen 15:19-21</reference>), not have been descendants of Ham at all. The common explanation of the name Perizzite as equivalent to פּרזות ארץ ישׁב “inhabitant of the level ground” (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.11">Eze 38:11</reference>), is at variance not only with the form of the word, the inhabitant of the level ground being called הפּרזי (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference>), but with the fact of their combination sometimes with the Canaanites, sometimes with the other tribes of Canaan, whose names were derived from their founders. Moreover, to explain the term “Canaanite,” as denoting “the civilised inhabitants of towns,” or “the trading Phoenicians,” is just as arbitrary as if we were to regard the Kenites, Kenizzites, and the other tribes mentioned Gen 15:19. along with the Canaanites, as all alike traders or inhabitants of towns. The origin of the name Perizzite is involved in obscurity, like that of the Kenites and other tribes settled in Canaan that were not descended from Ham. But we may infer from the frequency with which they are mentioned in connection with the Hamitic inhabitants of Canaan, that they were widely dispersed among the latter. Vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.15.19">Gen 15:19</reference>-21.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.13.8-Gen.13.9">Gen 13:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen208" type="x-p"/> To put an end to the strife between their herdsmen, Abram proposed to Lot that they should separate, as strife was unseemly between אחים אנשׁים, men who stood in the relation of brethren, and left him to choose his ground. “<hi type="italic">If thou to the left, I will turn to the right; and if thou to the right, I will turn to the left</hi>.” Although Abram was the older, and the leader of the company, he was magnanimous enough to leave the choice to his nephew, who was the younger, in the confident assurance that the Lord would so direct the decision, that His promise would be fulfilled.
entries.content_plain:
Gen 13:8-9 
 
 To put an end to the strife between their herdsmen, Abram proposed to Lot that they should separate, as strife was unseemly between אחים אנשׁים, men who stood in the relation of brethren, and left him to choose his ground. “If thou to the left, I will turn to the right; and if thou to the right, I will turn to the left.” Although Abram was the older, and the leader of the company, he was magnanimous enough to leave the choice to his nephew, who was the younger, in the confident assurance that the Lord would so direct the decision, that His promise would be fulfilled.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.13.10-Gen.13.13">Gen 13:10-13</reference> <div eID="gen208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen209" type="x-p"/> Lot chose what was apparently the best portion of the land, the whole district of the Jordan, or the valley on both sides of the Jordan from the Lake of Gennesareth to what was then the vale of Siddim. For previous to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, this whole country was well watered, “<hi type="italic">as the garden of Jehovah,</hi>” the garden planted by <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> in paradise, and “<hi type="italic">as Egypt,</hi>” the land rendered so fertile by the overflowing of the Nile, “<hi type="italic">in the direction of Zoar</hi>.” Abram therefore remained in the land of Canaan, whilst Lot settled in the cities of the plain of the Jordan, and tented (pitched his tents) as far as Sodom. In anticipation of the succeeding history (Gen 19), it is mentioned here (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">Gen 13:13</reference>), that the inhabitants of Sodom were very wicked, and sinful before <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>.

Gen 13:10-13

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.13.14-Gen.13.18">Gen 13:14-18</reference> <div eID="gen209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen210" type="x-p"/> After Lot’s departure, <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> repeated to Abram (by a mental, inward assurance, as we may infer from the fact that אמר “said” is not accompanied by ויּרא “he appeared”) His promise that He would give the land to him and to his seed in its whole extent, northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward, and would make his seed innumerable like the dust of the earth. From this we may see that the separation of Lot was in accordance with the will of God, as Lot had no share in the promise of God; though God afterwards saved him from destruction for Abram’s sake. The possession of the land is promised עולם עד “<hi type="italic">for ever</hi>.” The promise of God is unchangeable. As the seed of Abraham was to exist before God for ever, so Canaan was to be its everlasting possession. But this applied not to the lineal posterity of Abram, to his seed according to the flesh, but to the true spiritual seed, which embraced the promise in faith, and held it in a pure believing heart. The promise, therefore, neither precluded the expulsion of the unbelieving seed from the land of Canaan, nor guarantees to existing Jews a return to the earthly Palestine after their conversion to Christ. For as <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> justly says, “<hi type="italic">quam terra in saeculum promittitur, non simpliciter notatur perpetuitas; sed quae finem accepit in Christo</hi>.” Through Christ the promise has been exalted from its temporal form to its true essence; through Him the whole earth becomes Canaan (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.17.8">Gen 17:8</reference>). That Abram might appropriate this renewed and now more fully expanded promise, <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> directed him to walk through the land in the length of it and the breadth of it. In doing this he came in his “<hi type="italic">tenting</hi>,” i.e., his wandering through the land, to Hebron, where he settled by the terebinth of the Amorite Mamre (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.13">Gen 14:13</reference>), and built an altar to <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>. The term ישׁב (set himself, settled down, sat, dwelt) denotes that Abram made this place the central point of his subsequent stay in Canaan (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13">Gen 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.1">Gen 18:1</reference>, and Gen 23). On Hebron, see Gen 23:2. The war, which furnished Abram with an opportunity, while in the promised land of which as yet he could not really call a single rood his own, to prove himself a valiant warrior, and not only to smite the existing chiefs of the imperial power of Asia, but to bring back to the kings of Canaan the booty that had been carried off, is circumstantially described, not so much in the interests of secular history as on account of its significance in relation to the kingdom of God. It is of importance, however, as a simple historical fact, to see that in the statement in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen 14:1</reference>, the king of Shinar occupies the first place, although the king of Edom, Chedorlaomer, not only took the lead in the expedition, and had allied himself for that purpose with the other kings, but had previously subjugated the cities of the valley of Siddim, and therefore had extended his dominion very widely over hither Asia. If, notwithstanding this, the time of the war related here is connected with “<hi type="italic">the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar,</hi>” this is done, no doubt, with reference to the fact that the first worldly kingdom was founded in Shinar by Nimrod (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>), a kingdom which still existed under Amraphel, though it was now confined to Shinar itself, whilst Elam possessed the supremacy in inner Asia. There is no ground whatever for regarding the four kings mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen 14:1</reference> as four Assyrian generally or viceroys, as Josephus has done in direct contradiction to the biblical text; for, according to the more careful historical researches, the commencement of the Assyrian kingdom belongs to a later period; and <hi type="italic">Berosus</hi> speaks of an earlier Median rule in Babylon, which reaches as far back as the age of the patriarchs (cf. <hi type="italic">M. v. Niebuhr, Gesch. Assurs,</hi> p. 271). It appears significant also, that the imperial power of Asia had already extended as far as Canaan, and had subdued the valley of the Jordan, no doubt with the intention of holding the Jordan valley as the high-road to Egypt. We have here a prelude of the future assault of the worldly power upon the kingdom of God established in Canaan; and the importance of this event to sacred history consists in the fact, that the kings of the valley of the Jordan and the surrounding country submitted to the worldly power, whilst Abram, on the contrary, with his home-born servants, smote the conquerors and rescued their booty, - a prophetic sign that in the conflict with the power of the world the seed of Abram would not only not be subdued, but would be able to rescue from destruction those who appealed to it for aid.  <chapter eID="Gen.13"/> <div eID="gen210" type="x-p"/>
